unit.title: Coordinates, Patterns, Functions & Linear Relationships
unit.essential_question: How can coordinates, patterns, tables, graphs, equations, and words describe the same relationship—and how do we judge whether a linear model is useful?
big_ideas: Coordinates locate points by horizontal and vertical position.
A function assigns exactly one output to each allowed input.
Tables, graphs, equations, and words can represent the same relationship.
Slope describes rate of change, while an intercept describes an initial or boundary value.
Linear models support prediction only within a stated domain and with attention to error and limitations.
unit.architecture: Open-age integrated Pre-Algebra learning: coordinates + patterns + relations/functions + multiple representations + rate of change + slope/intercepts + linear/nonlinear reasoning + modelling/residuals + mastery
unit.tool_integration: Graphing and scientific-calculator tools may support plotting, arithmetic verification, and model checking after students define variables, show the relationship, and explain rate/intercept meaning.
unit.readiness_note: Unit 10 develops function and linear-model readiness for learners of any age. Advancement is based on demonstrated mastery, not grade identity.

lessons.title: Coordinate Plane, Ordered Pairs & Quadrants
objectives: Plot and read ordered pairs in all four quadrants.
Identify axes, origin, coordinates, and quadrants.
Interpret horizontal and vertical changes.
Use coordinates in maps, designs, and data displays.
warmup: Plot (3,2) and describe the horizontal move first.
Which coordinate is zero for every point on the y-axis?
Name the quadrant containing (−4,5).

concepts.heading: Coordinates are ordered
concepts.body: An ordered pair (x,y) gives horizontal position first and vertical position second.

concepts.heading: Axes divide the plane
concepts.body: The x-axis and y-axis meet at the origin and create four quadrants with predictable sign patterns.

concepts.heading: Scale controls interpretation
concepts.body: A graph may count by ones, tens, decimals, time intervals, or measured units; always read the scale.

steps: Move 3 units left from the origin.
examples.answer: The point lies in Quadrant II.

steps: State the distance in graph units.

examples.problem: Describe a point on the negative y-axis.
steps: A point on the y-axis has x=0.
Negative y-values lie below the origin.

pathways.Core: Plot, read, compare, and interpret coordinates in varied scales.
pathways.Extended: Analyze transformations, distance patterns, and coordinate constraints.

questions.explanation: Negative x and positive y identify Quadrant II.

lessons.title: Patterns, Sequences & Rules
objectives: Recognize arithmetic patterns and constant differences.
Describe recursive and explicit rules.
Generate terms from a rule.
Connect visual, numeric, and contextual patterns.
warmup: Find the next two terms in 5,9,13,…
Describe how 20,17,14,… changes.
Evaluate 3n+2 when n=4.

concepts.heading: A sequence has ordered terms
concepts.body: Each term has a position. Arithmetic sequences change by the same amount from one term to the next.

concepts.heading: Recursive rules build from earlier terms
concepts.body: A recursive rule states a starting term and how to obtain the next term.

concepts.heading: Explicit rules jump to any term
concepts.body: An explicit rule uses the term number n to calculate a chosen term directly.

steps: Interpret the result as the eighth term.
Verify both produce the same first terms.
examples.answer: The sequence 6,10,14,… can be written a₁=6, aₙ=aₙ₋₁+4 or aₙ=4n+2.

pathways.Foundation: Use tiles, tables, and repeated-addition arrows.
pathways.Core: Move among sequence lists, tables, recursive rules, and explicit rules.
pathways.Extended: Derive rules from geometric patterns and compare multiple valid forms.

lessons.application: Analyze a growing design, savings schedule, seating pattern, or repeated measurement. State what changes and what stays constant.

questions.explanation: The sequence begins at 4 and increases by 6.

lessons.title: Relations, Inputs, Outputs & the Function Concept
objectives: Interpret relations as sets of input-output pairs.
Determine whether a relation is a function.
Identify domain and range.
Evaluate function rules and interpret variables.
warmup: List the inputs in {(1,4),(2,7),(3,10)}.
Can one function input have two different outputs?
Evaluate f(3)=2(3)−1.

concepts.heading: A relation pairs values
concepts.body: A relation connects inputs to outputs through ordered pairs, a table, a mapping, a graph, or a rule.

concepts.heading: Functions assign one output per input
concepts.body: Different inputs may share an output, but one input cannot be paired with two different outputs.

concepts.heading: Domain and range describe allowed values
concepts.body: The domain contains inputs. The range contains resulting outputs.

steps: Check whether any input repeats with a different output.
Write function notation with the result.
Time t is selected or controlled.
examples.answer: t is independent; d is dependent.

pathways.Foundation: Use input-output machines, mapping arrows, and duplicate-input checks.
pathways.Core: Identify functions across ordered pairs, tables, graphs, and rules.
pathways.Extended: Analyze restricted domains, inverse relations, and function composition readiness.

lessons.application: Choose a rule involving time, cost, distance, temperature, or production. Define the input, output, domain, range, and why the relation is or is not a function.

questions.prompt: Which relation is not a function?

questions.explanation: The domain is the set of first coordinates.

questions.prompt: In distance as a function of time, the independent variable is usually:

questions.explanation: A set lists distinct output values.

lessons.title: Tables, Graphs, Equations & Verbal Representations
objectives: Translate among tables, graphs, equations, and words.
Generate a table from a rule.
Determine whether representations describe the same relationship.
Interpret constants and coefficients in context.
warmup: Complete y=2x+1 for x=0,1,2.
Write “start at 12 and add 5 per unit” as an equation.
Does (2,2) satisfy y=−x+4?

concepts.heading: Representations emphasize different features
concepts.body: Tables show sample values, graphs show shape and trend, equations support calculation, and words explain context.

concepts.heading: Equivalent representations agree
concepts.body: Every displayed pair from a table or graph must satisfy the equation and the verbal rule.

concepts.heading: Context gives symbols meaning
concepts.body: A coefficient may represent a rate; a constant may represent a starting value.

examples.problem: Create a table for y=3x+4 at x=0,1,2.

pathways.Foundation: Use paired tables and color-code the rate and starting value.
pathways.Core: Translate accurately among all four representations.
pathways.Extended: Compare equivalent forms and critique misleading graph scales.

lessons.application: Represent one public or fictional relationship in words, a table, an equation, and a graph. Explain what each representation reveals best.

questions.prompt: A table has (0,4),(1,7),(2,10). The rule is:
questions.explanation: The starting value is 4 and the rate is 3.

questions.prompt: “Start with 12 and add 5 per unit x” is:
questions.explanation: Rate times input plus starting value.

questions.prompt: Which representation best shows overall shape immediately?
questions.explanation: A graph makes shape and trend visible.

lessons.title: Rate of Change from Tables, Graphs & Contexts
objectives: Calculate rate of change from tables and points.
Interpret positive, negative, and zero rates.
Attach units to a rate.
Recognize constant versus changing rates.
warmup: Find Δy/Δx from (2,7) to (6,15).
What does a negative rate mean in a water-level context?
State units for distance per time.

concepts.heading: Rate compares two changes
concepts.body: Rate of change is change in output divided by change in input.

concepts.heading: The sign communicates direction
concepts.body: Positive rates increase, negative rates decrease, and zero rates stay constant as input changes.

concepts.heading: Units complete the meaning
concepts.body: A rate such as 5 has little meaning until it is described as dollars per item, meters per second, or another unit ratio.

examples.problem: Interpret a slope of −2 liters per minute.
examples.answer: Volume decreases by 2 liters each minute.

examples.problem: Determine whether a table is linear.
examples.answer: A constant rate indicates a linear relationship.

pathways.Foundation: Use change arrows and unit-rate tables.
pathways.Core: Calculate and interpret rates from tables, graphs, points, and contexts.
pathways.Extended: Compare average and local rates and analyze scale effects.

lessons.application: Estimate a rate from travel, temperature, growth, cost, water use, or production data. Include units and explain whether the rate appears constant.

questions.prompt: A negative rate means the output generally:
questions.explanation: Negative change indicates decrease as input increases.

questions.prompt: Distance divided by time is commonly measured in:

lessons.title: Slope, Intercepts & Linear Equations
objectives: Calculate slope from two points.
Interpret rise, run, and slope sign.
Identify x- and y-intercepts.
Write and interpret equations in slope-intercept form.
warmup: Find slope from (1,2) to (4,8).
Identify slope and y-intercept in y=−3x+5.
What is special about the slope of a vertical line?

concepts.heading: Slope is rise over run
concepts.body: For two points, slope compares vertical change to horizontal change.

concepts.heading: The y-intercept is an initial value
concepts.body: In y=mx+b, b is the output when x=0.

concepts.heading: Direction creates special slopes
concepts.body: Horizontal lines have slope 0; vertical lines have undefined slope because run is zero.

examples.problem: Write a line with slope 3 and y-intercept 4.

pathways.Foundation: Use slope triangles and intercept markers on grid paper.
pathways.Core: Calculate, graph, and interpret m and b across representations.
pathways.Extended: Write equations from varied conditions and compare parallel lines.

lessons.application: Model a fixed fee plus a rate, an elevation profile, a temperature change, or a resource balance. Interpret slope and intercept with units.

questions.prompt: In y=−3x+5, slope and y-intercept are:

questions.explanation: A vertical line has zero run.

questions.prompt: A line parallel to y=2x+1 has slope:
questions.explanation: Parallel nonvertical lines have equal slopes.

lessons.title: Linear vs Nonlinear Relationships & Function Notation
objectives: Distinguish linear and nonlinear relationships.
Use constant first differences as evidence.
Evaluate and interpret function notation.
Identify proportional relationships as a special linear case.
warmup: Is y=x² linear? Explain.
Evaluate f(−2) for f(x)=3x+1.
Does y=4x pass through the origin?

concepts.heading: Linear relationships have constant rate
concepts.body: Equal input changes produce equal output changes, and the graph is a straight line.

concepts.heading: Nonlinear relationships change rate
concepts.body: Curves, changing first differences, and variable slopes indicate nonlinearity.

concepts.heading: Function notation names an output
concepts.body: f(x) means the output of function f for input x; it does not mean f multiplied by x.

steps: The ratio y/x is 4 for nonzero x.

pathways.Foundation: Use straightedge checks, first-difference tables, and input-output substitution.
pathways.Core: Classify relationships and use function notation across tables, graphs, and equations.
pathways.Extended: Compare linear, quadratic, exponential, and piecewise behavior qualitatively.

lessons.application: Compare two public or fictional data sets. Decide which is approximately linear and justify using rate, graph shape, or first differences.

questions.prompt: Which output list has constant first differences?

questions.explanation: The squared input produces changing rate.

questions.prompt: The relation x=4 is not y as a function of x because:
questions.explanation: The vertical line gives many outputs for x=4.
A proportional linear relationship passes through the origin.

lessons.title: Linear Modelling, Prediction & Residual Analysis
objectives: Build a linear model from context or data.
Interpret slope and intercept in a model.
Distinguish interpolation from extrapolation.
Calculate and interpret residuals and limitations.
warmup: Interpret 25 in C=25+8h.
Is predicting at x=6 interpolation if data run from x=0 to x=10?
Find residual when observed is 52 and predicted is 49.

concepts.heading: Models simplify reality
concepts.body: A linear model captures an approximate constant-rate trend, not every detail.

concepts.heading: Interpolation is usually safer
concepts.body: Predictions inside the observed domain rely less on untested assumptions than extrapolations beyond it.

concepts.heading: Residuals measure prediction error
concepts.body: Residual = observed value − predicted value. Positive residuals lie above the model.

steps: Notice the prediction lies outside it.
examples.answer: Report the prediction cautiously and name the limitation.

pathways.Foundation: Use context tables, plotted points, and predicted-versus-observed comparisons.
pathways.Core: Build, interpret, test, and communicate linear models.
pathways.Extended: Compare candidate lines, residual patterns, and piecewise alternatives.

lessons.application: Use public, fictional, or measured data to create a transparent linear model. State domain, units, assumptions, residuals, and limits before making a recommendation.
